displayQuote: The Pope! How many divisions has he got?

meta.title: Who really said "The Pope! How many divisions has he got?"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Stalin in Churchill's 1948 memoir, which places it in Moscow with Laval in 1935. Churchill was not there, and rival Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam versions exist.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Pope! How many divisions has he got?'?
meta.ogDescription: Stalin's famous jibe comes to us secondhand, through Churchill's 1948 memoir about a 1935 Moscow meeting with Laval. Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam versions also circulated.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording first appears in Winston Churchill’s The Gathering Storm (1948). Churchill says Stalin said it to French foreign minister Pierre Laval in Moscow in 1935. Churchill heard the story from someone else and was not present, and no record by Stalin himself or by Laval has been found that contains these words.

source.heading: Where the words actually appear

docMeta.dd: The Second World War, Vol. I: The Gathering Storm
Winston S. Churchill (reporting, not a witness)
Ch. VIII, “Challenge and Response, 1935”; p. 121 in the Cassell 3rd edition (1950)

source.excerpt: Laval said: “Can’t you do something to encourage religion and the Catholics in Russia? It would help me so much with the Pope.” “Oho!” said Stalin. “The Pope! How many divisions has he got?” Laval’s answer was not reported to me; but he might certainly have mentioned a number of legions not always visible on parade.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Stalin. It says he said it sarcastically to Pierre Laval in 1935 and cites The Second World War (1948) by Winston Churchill, vol. 1, ch. 8 — Wikiquote: Joseph Stalin ↗

The Cassell edition of The Gathering Storm contains the exact exchange: Laval asks about encouraging Catholics in Russia, and Stalin answers “The Pope! How many divisions has he got?” — Internet Archive scan ↗

Word Histories found newspaper versions from before Churchill’s book, starting with a Time report of 27 December 1943 set at Tehran. Several papers in 1944–45 called the story apocryphal — Word Histories ↗
source.excerptNote: Churchill introduces the exchange as “a fragment not hitherto published” of Laval’s talks in Moscow. This text was checked against the Cassell third edition (1950) scanned by the Digital Library of India, which is the page number given above. The 1948 first editions may be paginated differently.

source.rightsNote: These words exist only in Churchill’s English-language The Gathering Storm, first published in 1948. A 1948 work by an identifiable author is treated as in copyright in the US, so the short excerpt here is quoted for commentary. No Russian-language original of Stalin’s remark has been documented.

author.name: Joseph Stalin
author.heading: About Joseph Stalin
author.metaLine: 1878–1953 · General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party, 1922–1952
author.bio: Joseph Stalin led the Soviet Union from the 1920s until he died in March 1953. He was General Secretary of the Communist Party from 1922 and also head of government from 1941. His reputation as a cold realist about power made him an obvious person to hang a line like this on. The line has followed him for decades, even though the only detailed account of it comes from a third party.

misattribution.heading: Three other settings, all shakier
misattribution.intro: Before Churchill’s memoir came out, the jibe was already going around with different settings and different people raising the Pope.

items.why: Time (27 December 1943) passed on a version attributed to Jan Smuts in which Churchill suggested involving the Pope, and Stalin asked “How many divisions has he?” Columnists in 1944 and 1945 called the story “Legend rather than Fact” and “undoubtedly apocryphal” — Word Histories ↗

items.who: Stalin at the Big Three conference
items.why: Newspapers in 1945–46 set the remark at Yalta. James F. Byrnes, who was at Yalta, wrote that “The Marshal did not make the statement at Yalta” — Word Histories ↗

items.who: Stalin addressing Churchill, as Truman told it
items.why: In 1948 Harry Truman set it at Potsdam, with Stalin asking Churchill how many divisions he said the Pope had. That differs from Churchill’s own account, published the same year — Word Histories ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The detailed source for the familiar wording is Churchill’s The Gathering Storm (1948), which sets it in Moscow in 1935 with Pierre Laval. Churchill had the story from someone else (“Laval’s answer was not reported to me”), so it is a credible attribution but not a verified one — Internet Archive scan ↗

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: In Churchill’s telling, Stalin and Molotov had just been pressing Laval on hard military numbers: how many French divisions there would be and how long men would serve. Laval then asked whether something could be done for Catholics in Russia to help him with the Pope. Stalin’s reply turns the conversation’s own unit of measure against the Vatican. That is a big part of why the line became shorthand for the gap between moral authority and military force.

Churchill added his own reply on Laval’s behalf, saying Laval “might certainly have mentioned a number of legions not always visible on parade.” Later retellings kept adding comebacks. One of them, reported in 1958, is a supposed reply from Pius XII that Stalin would meet his divisions in heaven.
